passage: Rehana, fifteen, lived above her father's cloth shop in Bijnor, and for months the headaches had kept coming back, a tight band behind her eyes. On the evening of her friend Lakshmi's mehendi, Rehana lay in the dark with a wet cloth on her forehead instead. "She's just moody," her Phuphi said from the doorway. "It's nothing. Girls her age make excuses." Rehana turned her face to the wall, hot with anger and shame. Lakshmi sent a voice note: "Missed you. Is it the headache again?" That night Abbu sat on the edge of the bed. "Nothing that keeps coming back is nothing. Tomorrow we go to the doctor in town." The doctor listened to every detail, wrote it all down and made a plan to find out more. On the bus home, Rehana's head still hurt a little, but she felt lighter. Someone believed her.

qa.q: What did Rehana lie with on her forehead?
qa.a: A wet cloth.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when Phuphi called it nothing?
qa.a: She felt angry and ashamed, hurt at being dismissed when the pain was real.

qa.q: What made the biggest difference for Rehana, and why?
qa.a: Abbu taking her seriously and going to the doctor, who listened and planned to find out more; being believed lightened the emotional weight.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi seem to see Rehana missing the mehendi?
qa.a: Lakshmi misses her but understands, gently asking if it is the headache again instead of taking offence.

grounding: Shows a teenager with frequent headaches missing plans and feeling misunderstood when told it is nothing, then being taken seriously and properly checked.

passage: Freya had cancelled on Hiroshi three Saturdays running. Headaches, again. In their Glasgow kitchen her dad sighed, "It's all that screen time, love. You're just in a mood." Freya stomped upstairs, slammed her door, then cried into her pillow, which made her head pound harder. That night Hiroshi messaged: "You don't have to explain. Is your head really bad? Have you seen someone about it?" Freya read it twice. Nobody had asked like that. Next morning she told her mum how often it happened and how it made her feel like a liar. Her mum rang the doctor's surgery that day. At the appointment the GP asked careful questions, took notes and arranged some checks. "We'll work this out together," she said. Freya walked out still sore, but for the first time in weeks, not alone with it.

qa.q: Who rang the doctor's surgery?
qa.a: Freya's mum.

qa.q: How did Freya feel when her dad blamed screen time?
qa.a: She felt dismissed and angry, then upset enough to cry, because the pain was real.

qa.q: What helped Freya most, and why?
qa.a: Hiroshi's kind question, then telling her mum and seeing the GP; being taken seriously and checked properly eased the loneliness of the pain.

qa.q: How does Hiroshi respond to the cancelled Saturdays?
qa.a: Hiroshi does not take them personally, and instead asks with care whether Freya's head is bad and whether anyone has checked it.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager with recurring headaches cancelling plans and feeling dismissed, and relief when she is believed and properly checked.

passage:
"Santosh, Rohit's at the gate. Cricket?"
"Not today, Amma."
"That's the fourth time this month. What's going on? Always sulking in this dark room."
"I'm not sulking. My head hurts."
"Again? It's nothing, kanna. Drink water, you'll be fine."
"You always say it's nothing! It's behind my eyes, almost every day after school. I can't even read the board without squinting."
"Every day?"
"Most days. I stopped telling you because you'd just say drink water."
"Lavanya, come here. Listen to your brother."
"Anna, why didn't you tell me? You've been snapping at everyone."
"Because nobody believes me."
"I believe you. I'm sorry, Santosh. Tomorrow we'll go to Dr. Menon, and get your eyes checked too."
"Really?"
"Really. And no cricket until we know. Just rest."

qa.q: How often does Santosh say his head hurts?
qa.a: Most days, behind his eyes, after school.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when Amma said it was nothing?
qa.a: He felt hurt and misunderstood, as if nobody believed him, which is why he had stopped telling anyone.

qa.q: What changed once Amma took him seriously?
qa.a: She believed him, apologised and planned a proper check with the doctor and an eye test, which eased the weight he had been carrying alone.

qa.q: How had Lavanya experienced Santosh's moods?
qa.a: Lavanya had seen him snapping at everyone without knowing he was in pain, and wished he had told her.

grounding: Shows a teenager with frequent headaches seeming moody and avoiding plans, feeling dismissed, and relieved once believed and taken for a check.

passage: Last year I became the friend who always cancelled. I'm Urmila, and for about four months I had headaches almost every afternoon, a tight band round my forehead that made light and noise feel sharp. I skipped Lakshmi's birthday picnic and the school trip, and people started saying I'd turned moody and stuck-up. My uncle said it was "just exam stress, everyone gets it". I believed him for a while and felt stupid for complaining. Then one evening I cried at dinner because the TV was too loud, and Papa put it on mute and said, "Tell me properly." The next week he took me to a doctor, who listened for a long time and asked me to keep a headache diary. We found patterns and made a plan. The headaches didn't vanish overnight, but being believed took half the weight off at once. I phoned Lakshmi and explained. "Why didn't you say?" was all she asked.

qa.q: What did the doctor ask Urmila to keep?
qa.a: A headache diary.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when told it was just exam stress?
qa.a: Urmila felt stupid and misunderstood, doubting whether the pain was real enough to complain about.

qa.q: What helped most, according to Urmila?
qa.a: Being believed and properly checked: Papa listened, the doctor took time and suggested a headache diary, and a plan followed.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi have felt about the missed birthday picnic?
qa.a: Lakshmi may have felt hurt or puzzled at the time, and later wished Urmila had explained.

grounding: Shows a teenager with frequent headaches cancelling plans and being called moody, and the relief of being taken seriously and checked.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Monday
Tushar has missed PE twice this month and sits in the back row with his hood up. Some staff have called him lazy and moody. Today he snapped at a classmate who was drumming on the desk, then put his head down. When I spoke to him privately, he said he gets headaches most days, and when he told his coach, he was told, "It's nothing, toughen up." He looked close to tears saying it. I told him I believed him and that pain like that deserves a proper check. With his permission I called his mother this afternoon; she hadn't realised how often it was happening and is booking him with their doctor this week. I've asked staff to let him sit away from the window glare for now.
Vinita

qa.q: Where does Tushar sit in class?
qa.a: In the back row, with his hood up.

qa.q: What did Tushar feel when his coach said "It's nothing, toughen up"?
qa.a: He felt hurt and dismissed, close to tears, as if his pain did not count.

qa.q: What made Vinita's response helpful?
qa.a: Vinita believed him, spoke privately, told his mother the same day so he could see a doctor, and eased the glare in class.

qa.q: How might Tushar's mother feel after the call?
qa.a: Surprised and concerned, not having realised how often the headaches came.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose frequent headaches make him seem moody and withdrawn, feeling dismissed, and an adult who believes him and arranges a check.

passage:
Thursday
Headache again, the third this week. It starts behind my eyes after school, and by evening it's like a band squeezing my head. I skipped Sana's birthday because the music would have made it worse, and now the group thinks I'm stuck-up. At dinner Chachu said, 'Teenagers and their dramas. It's nothing.' I went to my room and cried, which made it worse.
Then Urmila Khala knocked. She sat on my bed, didn't say anything silly, just asked when it started and what helps. She said, 'Pain that keeps coming back deserves a proper check-up. We'll go to the doctor on Saturday.' I felt so relieved I almost cried again.
Zeenat

qa.q: When will Zeenat and Urmila Khala go to the doctor?
qa.a: On Saturday.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel when Chachu called it drama?
qa.a: Zeenat felt hurt and misunderstood, so upset that crying made the headache worse.

qa.q: What did Urmila Khala do that helped?
qa.a: She listened calmly, asked when it started and what helps, and arranged a proper check-up.

qa.q: How might the friends see Zeenat skipping the birthday?
qa.a: They may see Zeenat as stuck-up, not knowing the headache made the music unbearable.

grounding: A teenager with frequent headaches avoids plans and feels dismissed until an adult takes it seriously and arranges a check-up.
